plurals.name: root_grant_shared
plurals.item: This app shares its user ID with %1$d other app; Root access applies to it too.
This app shares its user ID with %1$d other apps; Root access applies to all of them.

resources.string: These are the values KernelSU applies to this app\'s su sessions. KernelSU\'s profile templates and extra SELinux rules for a custom domain are not offered: they need its manager app, and a rule set loaded from here would change the whole system\'s SELinux policy. Turning Root access off returns the profile to the default.
Confirm it\'s you to give %1$s Root access
Confirm it\'s you to widen what Root access lets %1$s do
Allowing Root access, and every profile change that widens what it may do, ask for your screen lock or fingerprint first
Set a screen lock to have Root access ask for it, or continue with the confirmation you gave just now.
This phone has no screen lock, so your identity cannot be checked. Tap to set one.
Your identity cannot be checked on this phone at the moment. Tap for the screen lock settings.
Allow only apps you trust. An app with Root access can read all data, change the system and hide what it does.
%1$s will be able to run any command as Root, with full control over this device and all its data.
%1$s runs as a system identity (user ID %2$d). If you allow it, every process with this identity can run any command as Root.
%1$s is the shell identity (user ID 2000) that adb uses. If you allow it, every computer authorized for USB or wireless debugging gets full Root access, as with Rooted debugging in Developer options.

%1$s runs as the system user (user ID 1000), which Android\'s system server and many system apps share. If you allow it, every process with this identity can run any command as Root, and a flaw in any of them gives full control of the device outside SELinux\'s protection.
Apps allowed here can run commands as Root (su), which gives full control over this device.
Root sessions work in the system\'s global mount namespace; their mounts are visible to every app
Each Root session gets its own copy of the mounts; its changes stay private
Root sessions see the mounts of the app that starts them
An SELinux context of the form user:role:type:level, such as u:r:shell:s0. The system checks that its policy has it; a domain without the rules its programs need makes su sessions fail.
Android\'s su domain; exists only on debuggable builds
Su sessions of this app run with this group ID. 0 is root.
Group IDs to add, separated by commas.
Programs in a su session cannot call su again to regain this profile
Su sessions of %1$s get KernelSU\'s default Root profile again.
KernelSU\'s default: user and group 0, every capability, KernelSU\'s domain, inherited mount namespace
Su sessions of this app run with this user ID. 0 is root; another ID leaves them without root\'s file access.

KernelSU applies these values exactly as chosen. A narrower user ID, group set, capability set or SELinux domain makes most programs that ask for su fail; a wrong value can leave this app\'s su sessions unusable until the default profile is restored here.
User ID %1$d is shared with %2$s. KernelSU grants Root access per user ID, so it applies to all of them.
Allowed: the app can run commands as Root
Not available: KernelSU does not grant Root access to system identities below user ID 2000 other than 1000 (this app: %1$d)
Not available: Lujarch\'s own apps never get Root access
These values can\'t be a root profile
This app can\'t get Root access
This app has no Root access
Apps that can run commands as Root
Root, su, superuser, Root access, KernelSU
Root sessions is on: sessions as root in Arch Linux and in Android
